A playwright who solves the dilemma of characters by rescuing them from impossible circumstances using an extra-human device has employed deus ex machina. This term, Latin for god from the machine, originated in ancient Greek theatre where a crane would lower a god figure onto the stage to resolve an impossible plot situation. It describes any artificial, contrived resolution brought in from outside the play's natural logic.

When a protagonist is purged of the dominant emotions of pity and fear at the end of a tragedy, it is called catharsis. Derived from Aristotle's Poetics, catharsis refers to the emotional purification or release that audiences experience by living vicariously through the protagonist's suffering. Watching tragedy provokes and then releases pity and fear, leaving the audience cleansed and emotionally balanced.

When a statement is made on stage to the hearing of only the audience and not the other characters, it is called an aside. The aside is a theatrical convention in which a character briefly breaks from the scene to address the audience directly, revealing thoughts or information that other characters cannot hear. It creates intimacy between actor and audience and enables dramatic irony.

The passage reveals that Otto's wife was a potter in addition to being a wife and mother. Nessa reflects that the other women had defined themselves primarily through domestic roles, while Otto's wife maintained her identity as a professional potter alongside being a wife and mother. This combination, rather than replacement of one role for another, is what distinguishes her from the others.

The atmosphere of the reception for the third marriage is described as grandiose and joyful. The wedding celebration combines elements of grandeur and festivity, with the ancient custom being more than just respected suggesting an elaborate, ceremonial quality. The gathering is both magnificently large in scale and filled with genuine happiness, creating a compound atmosphere of grandeur and joy.

In Donne's Holy Sonnet, the persona saying SINCE I am coming to that Holy room where I shall be made thy music, I tune the Instrument here reveals that he is near his death. The holy room is heaven, and he is preparing his soul as a musician tunes an instrument before a performance. The sense of imminent arrival in the divine presence indicates that death is approaching.

Lawino's description in Okot p'Bitek's Song of Lawino that Ocol is in love with a modern woman who speaks English is critical of the modern woman. Lawino regards this modern, English-speaking woman as inferior to traditional African womanhood and Ocol's preference as a cultural betrayal. The poem implicitly criticizes the Westernized modern woman by contrasting her negatively with authentic African values.

In Okot p'Bitek's Song of Lawino, the line we could hear it faintly passing through the air uses personification. The song is given the human quality of passing, as if it moves deliberately through space like a person walking. This personification of the song as a presence traveling through the air gives it a ghostly, tangible quality that amplifies its emotional impact.

In The Trials of Brother Jero, Jero is aptly described as suave. His smoothness, polish, and effortless social grace in manipulating people are characteristic of the suave persona he cultivates. He moves with calculated charm, presenting a carefully constructed exterior of spiritual authority and refinement that conceals his fundamentally fraudulent nature.

In The Trials of Brother Jero, when Jero says this morning alone he has been thrice in conflict with the daughters of discord, the conflict that concerns him most is with Chume's wife Amope, whom he owes money. Amope is his creditor who is persistently pursuing him for repayment, and her presence represents the most immediate practical threat to Jero's comfortable existence.

At the opening of The Trials of Brother Jero, when a spotlight illuminates the dark stage, it reveals the prophet, Brother Jero himself. This theatrical staging choice, isolating Jero in a single beam of light against darkness, immediately establishes him as the central figure of the play and allows him to deliver his opening monologue to the audience, setting up his character before any other action begins.

The most immediate service that Jero wishes to saddle MEMBER with at the end of The Trials of Brother Jero is to use him to arrest Chume. Jero has manipulated the politician MEMBER and now plans to use his newly acquired political connection as a tool for his own purposes. Getting MEMBER to order the arrest of Chume, who has become dangerous to Jero's security, is his immediate practical goal.

In She Stoops to Conquer, the technique in which most characters act in ignorance while the audience is aware of the true situation is dramatic irony. The audience knows from the beginning that the Hardcastle home is not an inn and that Kate is not a barmaid, while Marlow and Hastings remain ignorant throughout much of the play. This sustained dramatic irony is the source of the play's sustained comic tension.

The most significant factors driving members to Jero's church in The Trials of Brother Jero are fulfillment and security. People come to Jero because they seek a sense of purpose, belonging, and safety from life's uncertainties. Jero expertly exploits this desire for spiritual fulfilment and the security of divine protection, offering his followers the emotional satisfaction of feeling spiritually cared for.

Kate agrees to her father's choice of a husband because of the suitor's reserved and bashful nature. Young Marlow's shyness with women of his own social class gives Kate an advantage in the relationship, allowing her to take control by stooping to conquer. She accepts the match partly because Marlow's bashfulness makes him a manageable prospect that her own wit and personality can work with.

Mrs Hardcastle is depicted as a potential aristocrat, someone who aspires to the higher social circles and fashionable life of the aristocracy. Her obsession with London fashions, her airs and pretensions, and her desire to marry her ward Neville well all reflect aspirations toward a more elevated social position than she actually holds. She performs aristocratic taste and sensibility while remaining a country gentlewoman.

For Young Marlow, the most objectionable aspect of marriage is the rigors of formal courtship. Marlow is paralyzed by shyness when meeting women of his own social class and finds the formal rituals of courtship, the careful conversation, the expected behavior, and the scrutiny of polite society utterly uncomfortable. This social anxiety makes formal courtship, rather than any other aspect of marriage, the most unpleasant obstacle for him.

She Stoops to Conquer is concerned principally with presenting the problems of social class and British mannerisms. Goldsmith satirizes the class-consciousness, social pretension, and rigid behavioral codes of eighteenth-century English society. Through the comedy of mistaken identities and social confusion, he exposes how class anxiety and the tyranny of social mannerisms distort human relationships and prevent natural behavior.

The conversation in which X describes someone as a man of excellent understanding and very generous is a conversation between Mr Hardcastle and Kate about Marlow. Hardcastle is speaking to his daughter about the young man he has chosen as her prospective husband, trying to sell her on Marlow's virtues before the young man arrives. This father-daughter discussion establishes the context for Kate's eventual encounter with Marlow.

Goldsmith's satire is most biting when applied to Mrs Hardcastle. She is the character who most fully embodies the social pretensions, fashionable affectation, and uncritical embrace of metropolitan culture that Goldsmith wishes to satirize. Her slavish following of London fashion, her indulgence of Tony, and her attempts at social climbing make her the primary target of the play's satirical edge.

The selected poem portrays its subject with sensitiveness and arrogance. These two qualities coexist in the character or persona described: a heightened emotional sensitivity combined with a prideful, disdainful attitude toward others. This combination creates a complex, contradictory figure who feels things deeply but expresses this feeling through a posture of superiority rather than vulnerability.

The selected poem identifies hunters as the focus of its concern. The poem deals with those who hunt, whether literally or metaphorically, exploring the role of the hunter in society, the relationship between hunter and prey, or the cultural significance of hunting. The hunters are the primary actors around whom the poem's imagery and argument are organized.

The primary function of the imagery in the selected poem is making us more conscious of the earth. The poem's images draw attention to the physical reality of the ground beneath our feet, the soil, the natural environment we inhabit and sometimes ignore. By making the earth vivid and palpable through imagery, the poem heightens our awareness of and connection to the natural world.

The selected poem is about slave labour. The poem addresses the experience of forced labor under oppressive conditions, examining the physical and psychological dimensions of being compelled to work against one's will. Whether addressing historical slavery or its contemporary equivalents, the poem engages with the dehumanizing reality of labor extracted through coercion.

The selected poem conveys a non-concern for space, suggesting that physical location or available room is not a priority for the speaker. The persona demonstrates an indifference to spatial constraints or living conditions, suggesting either philosophical detachment from material circumstances or a focused inner life that renders external spatial concerns irrelevant.

The selected poem deals with the inevitability of fate. The poem presents circumstances or outcomes as inescapable, suggesting that certain things are predetermined and cannot be avoided regardless of human effort or intention. This fatalistic perspective creates a tone of resigned acceptance, acknowledging that some forces exceed human capacity to resist or redirect.

The selected poem uses allegory as its dominant device. The poem tells a story or describes a situation in which the surface narrative carries a parallel, symbolic meaning about abstract ideas, political situations, or moral truths. Every element of the allegorical poem corresponds to a meaning outside the literal narrative, making the poem function on two simultaneous levels of meaning.

In Wordsworth's Solitary Reaper, the comparison of the reaper's song to the cuckoo-bird explores the relieving effect of the song on the reaper. The cuckoo's call brings relief and coolness after weary travel, and the comparison suggests that the reaper's song similarly provides emotional relief and refreshment, offering solace to both the singer and the overheard listener through its haunting, sad beauty.

In Robert Browning's My Last Duchess, the painting of the Duchess represents a perfectly realistic representation of her. The Duke refers to Fra Pandolf's painting as capturing the Duchess with absolute fidelity, so real that the painting seems alive. This realism in the portrait allows the Duke to continue controlling her image even after her death, possessing her perfect representation forever.

In The Stillborn, Li got more accustomed to her home because she became closer to tradition. Rather than continuing to resist or seek escape from her traditional environment, Li gradually developed a deeper acceptance of and connection to the traditional ways of her community. This accommodation to tradition reflects a maturation and rooting in the values she was initially eager to leave behind.

In The Stillborn, the lines my blood is hot, but my flesh is famished, the rains have come, the field is prepared express the agony of a wasted fertility. The speaker is biologically ready for motherhood or love, the blood hot and the field prepared, but nothing comes of it. The fertility remains unfulfilled, creating anguish at the waste of potential that is ready but finds no outlet.

In The Stillborn, the passage and in spite of everything, in the soft cradle of her heart, there was another baby forming refers to the reunion of Li and Habu. The baby forming in her heart symbolizes the rekindling of her love for Habu, a new beginning of their relationship. The image of a baby forming represents new emotional life and the possibility of reconciliation between the two characters.

The dominant tone of The Stillborn is one of anger. Despite the novel's surface focus on the disappointment of dreams and the challenges of village and city life, an undercurrent of anger at the social conditions, the limitations imposed on women, and the failures of individuals and society runs through the narrative. This anger motivates Alkali's critique of the forces that still birth human potential.

The major concern of The Stillborn is the promotion of simple, rural existence. The novel ultimately valorizes the village and the traditional way of life over the corrupting influence of the city. By showing how the city disappoints and destroys those who seek it as an escape, Alkali implicitly argues for the value of the simpler, more rooted rural existence that Li eventually returns to and embraces.

Grandma informs Li that her salt-pot is empty because grandfather will never part with his money for salt. The old man's miserliness means that even basic condiments like salt are not purchased, leaving the household without this essential. Grandma's complaint to Li is therefore a practical appeal rooted in the grandfather's extreme unwillingness to spend money on household necessities.

In The Mayor of Casterbridge, characterization is designed to show that man's fate is determined by his character. Henchard's downfall is not random misfortune but flows directly from his own personality: his pride, stubbornness, impulsiveness, and inability to control himself. Hardy demonstrates through Henchard that character is destiny, that who we fundamentally are creates the conditions for what happens to us.

The characters of Henchard and Farfrae in The Mayor of Casterbridge represent the contrast between the old and the new. Henchard embodies the old ways: impulsive, instinctive, traditional, and resistant to modern methods. Farfrae represents the new: scientific, rational, adaptable, and commercially modern. Their conflict dramatizes the broader tension between tradition and progress in Victorian England.

One of the main features that sustains the reader's interest in The Mayor of Casterbridge is the creation and resolution of conflicts. The novel generates tension through constantly evolving conflicts between characters and within Henchard himself, and the reader's engagement is maintained by the need to see how these conflicts will be resolved. Hardy creates new complications just as old ones are resolved, maintaining narrative momentum.

Hardy employs the character of Henchard to propagate the notion of confessing our weaknesses. Henchard's trajectory from pride through humiliation to eventual self-knowledge suggests that acknowledging one's fundamental weaknesses, however painful, is necessary for moral honesty. The novel follows Henchard's long, agonizing journey toward facing the truth about himself as the core of its moral argument.

The goal of The Mayor of Casterbridge is to expose the influence of environment and morality in human conduct. Hardy examines how the social environment of Casterbridge, with its economic pressures, community judgments, and moral codes, shapes the choices characters make and determines their fates. The novel demonstrates the powerful interplay between external circumstances and individual moral character.

Henchard arranged the meeting with Susan at the Ring rather than in his house because his reputation as church-warden and mayor was at stake. If Susan had come openly to his house, it would have raised questions about their relationship and potentially exposed his past. The Ring, a secluded ancient amphitheatre used for clandestine meetings, provided a discreet venue that protected his public standing.

A narrator that tells their story as if all actions revolve around them is a first-person narrator. When a narrator uses I and positions themselves at the center of every event, making everything relative to their own experience and perspective, they are using the first-person mode. This personal, self-centered narration creates intimacy but also limits the narrative to what the narrator can know and observe.

What makes The Mayor of Casterbridge a tragedy is the poetic justice in Henchard's punishment. Henchard's suffering is directly proportional to his wrongdoing: having sold his wife and daughter, he loses them again; having been dishonest and proud, he is exposed and humiliated. The punishment fits the crime with an exactness that constitutes poetic justice, giving the novel its tragic moral coherence.

An inherent quality of the lyric is that it must express the poet's subjective emotions. The lyric poem, unlike narrative or dramatic poetry, is fundamentally an expression of personal feeling, mood, and inner experience. The speaker's subjective emotional state is the poem's essential content, making the lyric a direct outpouring of individual feeling rather than a story told or a scene dramatized.

The literary term that describes the angle at which a writer tells their story is point of view. Point of view refers to the narrative perspective from which a story is told: who the narrator is, what they know, and how they relate to the events and characters. First person, third person omniscient, and third person limited are different points of view that shape the story's presentation fundamentally.

A satire employs sarcasm and humour for social criticism. Satire uses irony, wit, ridicule, and exaggeration to expose and critique human follies, vices, and social institutions. While it generates laughter, satire's ultimate purpose is moral and social correction, using the tools of comedy to hold up a critical mirror to society and encourage reform through the sting of recognizing one's own absurdities.

A character who remains unchanged throughout a work of art is called a flat character. Flat characters are defined by a single dominant trait or a limited set of qualities and do not develop or transform over the course of the narrative. They are often used as foils for more complex round characters, and their predictability serves plot purposes rather than psychological depth.

In J.P. Clark's Night Rain, the description of being doped out of the deep, having bobbed up bellywise like a fish uses onomatopoeia as its dominant device. The word bobbed imitates the sound and movement of rising and falling in water, creating an immediate sensory impression through the sound of the word itself. The onomatopoeic quality reinforces the drowsy, water-laden atmosphere of the poem.

A figure of speech in which an absent person or an object is addressed as if present is referred to as apostrophe. In apostrophe, the speaker directly addresses something or someone who is not literally present: a dead person, a personified abstraction, or a distant beloved. This device creates emotional intensity by making the absent entity immediate and responsive to the speaker's words.

The figure of speech in which a poet implicitly compares an object or idea with another totally different one is called a metaphor. A metaphor makes this comparison directly, asserting identity rather than similarity, without using like or as. By saying A is B, a metaphor fuses two different things in a way that reveals unexpected similarities, enriching both terms with the qualities of the other.

The lines I love to pass my fingers through the strands of your hair, dark as night, use a simile. The comparison of the hair's darkness to the night is introduced by as, making it an explicit comparison that uses the word as to signal the comparison. The simile dark as night creates a vivid, immediate image of deep, absolute darkness that characterizes the hair.

The repeated phrase as white people do in the poem about kissing is used for emphasis. By repeating the phrase after each action described, the poet underlines and stresses the imitative nature of the behavior, insisting that each act is being performed in imitation of white behavior. This emphatic repetition draws attention to the cultural mimicry being described, making the contrast between authentic and performed behavior clear.

When a writer refers to past events to throw light on current ones, they are employing flashback. Flashback is a narrative technique that interrupts the chronological flow to depict events from an earlier time, providing context, explanation, or contrast for the present situation. It allows writers to reveal relevant history without having to narrate events in strict chronological sequence.

The poem about the madman entering the house with violence, defiling sacred grounds, and bending down high priests with force is about coercion. The violent entry, the defiling of sacred space, and the forcible subjugation of religious authorities all describe the use of force to overcome resistance. Coercion is the dominant method described: compliance achieved through violence rather than consent or persuasion.

The branch of knowledge that places emphasis on beauty is aesthetics. Aesthetics is the philosophical study of beauty, art, and taste, concerned with questions about what makes things beautiful, how we perceive and judge aesthetic qualities, and what the nature and value of art is. As a branch of philosophy and criticism, aesthetics provides the theoretical framework for literary and artistic evaluation.

In Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, Obaseki's call for obedience from the auditorium reflects his attitude of refusal to pay homage to the whiteman. The context suggests that one of the chiefs is refusing to submit to British authority, and Obaseki, speaking from an unusual position in the auditorium, urges compliance for the peace of the land. The issue is whether the Benin chiefs will acknowledge British colonial authority.

In Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, the Oba's comment about a woman without a man taking another husband refers to the marital status of Queen Victoria. The Oba, upon learning that the British are ruled by a queen, is confused and makes a culturally specific observation about women without husbands needing to remarry. His comment reveals his inability to understand a female monarch governing independently, reflecting his own cultural assumptions about gender and leadership.

Wordsworth's Solitary Reaper uses the rhyme scheme abcbddee. The poem's stanzas alternate between unrhymed and rhymed lines in a pattern where the second and fourth lines rhyme (cb), then the stanza closes with two couplets (dd, ee). This irregular but patterned rhyme scheme gives the poem its distinctive musical quality appropriate to a meditation on a solitary singer's haunting song.

In Macbeth, the play reaches a turning point when Duncan is murdered in Macbeth's castle. The murder of King Duncan is the point of no return in the play: it is the action that commits Macbeth irrevocably to a path of further violence and deceit. After this moment, the moral corruption initiated by ambition becomes permanent, and the tragic consequences become inevitable.

In Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, the proverb the python seeking assurance of adulthood measures his length with the palm tree is addressed to The chiefs. Ovonramwen uses this proverb to address his chiefs, comparing himself or the kingdom to a python measuring itself against a tall tree. The proverb serves as a symbolic statement about the Oba's own stature and authority in the face of the British challenge.

In Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, the Oba's poetic language reveals his haughtiness. The elevated, metaphor-laden speech he uses reflects not just his cultural tradition of royal oratory but also his pride and sense of absolute authority. His language is that of a man accustomed to deference, who speaks with the confidence of one who has never had to accommodate others, revealing his aristocratic disdain and unbending pride.

In Macbeth, the step on which Macbeth must fall down or else o'erleap refers to his ambition to become King of Scotland. Malcolm's naming as Prince of Cumberland is an obstacle between Macbeth and the throne: either Macbeth accepts this setback (falls down) or he must act illegally to overcome it (o'erleap). The goal that makes this step an obstacle is the Scottish kingship.

The speech accursed be that tongue that tells me so, for it hath cowed my better part of man occurs when Macduff confronts Macbeth for the final battle. Macbeth hears that Macduff was not naturally born but was untimely ripped from his mother's womb, revealing that the witches' prophecy has been fulfilled. This revelation cows Macbeth's courage, triggering his defiant but despairing response.

It is dramatic irony that the castle which has a pleasant, gentle air happens to be the death-place of King Duncan. Duncan and Banquo admire the castle's atmosphere and praise its beauty just before Duncan is murdered inside it. The audience, who know that Duncan will be killed there, experience the irony of hearing him praise the very place that will become the scene of his murder.

The event described in the selected poem comes as unexpected. The poem presents something that happens without warning or preparation, taking both the characters within the poem and perhaps the reader by surprise. This quality of unexpectedness gives the event its dramatic impact and may carry thematic significance about the unpredictability of life or the failure of human foresight.

The selected poem suggests that the speaker lies on the fence between good and evil. The speaker is morally ambivalent, positioned between ethical poles without committing fully to either goodness or wickedness. This liminal moral position creates a complex, uncertain identity and reflects a broader condition of ethical paralysis or deliberate balance between opposing moral claims.

In Macbeth, Malcolm's speech about pouring the sweet milk of concord into hell and uproaring the universe suggests a desire to get power and authority at all cost. Malcolm is testing Macduff by exaggerating his own wickedness, claiming he would destroy peace itself to gain power. He describes an ambition so absolute that it would sacrifice harmony and order for the sake of domination.

The selected poem interprets or presents its subject metaphorically. The poem uses figurative rather than literal language to describe its subject, meaning that the surface description represents something other than what is literally named. This metaphorical approach enriches the poem's meaning by allowing concrete images to carry abstract or symbolic significance beyond their literal reference.

The central subject of the selected poem is bloodshed. The poem deals with violence, killing, and the physical reality of death through injury or warfare. Whether historical, personal, or communal, the poem's imagery and concern are organized around the theme of blood being shed and the human cost of violence, making bloodshed its primary thematic concern.

The attitude conveyed in the selected poem is hypocritical. The speaker or the subjects of the poem profess values or feelings that their actual behavior or circumstances contradict. This gap between professed and actual values defines hypocrisy, and the poem exposes this contradiction through its tone, imagery, or narrative, holding the hypocritical attitude up to critical scrutiny.

The selected poem uses the image of spiritual rebirth as its central symbol. The poem draws on imagery of renewal, transformation, and new life emerging from death or dormancy to explore themes of spiritual regeneration. Whether through religious imagery or secular metaphors of renewal, the poem is concerned with the possibility of being reborn to a new spiritual condition.

The selected poem describes an uneventful tour. The journey depicted is characterized by the absence of incident, excitement, or memorable experience. The lack of eventfulness is itself significant, suggesting either the tedium of travel, the monotony of experience, or a journey through a landscape or life that fails to produce the anticipated or hoped-for encounters and transformations.

The selected poem uses a paradox as its primary literary device. The poem presents a statement or situation that appears self-contradictory or impossible yet reveals a deeper truth upon reflection. This paradoxical quality gives the poem its intellectual depth, requiring readers to work through the apparent contradiction to discover the insight that reconciles the seemingly incompatible elements.

The theme of Ayi Kwei Armah's The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born is hatred. The novel is suffused with the hatred and contempt that moral failure, corruption, and compromise generate, both the hatred that the Man feels for the corrupt society around him and the disdain that society returns for his stubborn integrity. Hatred as a social and psychological condition pervades the novel's atmosphere.

The selected poem uses a bird as its central image. The bird, whether as a symbol of freedom, beauty, spiritual transcendence, or natural vitality, is the concrete image through which the poem develops its meaning. Birds in poetry carry rich associative possibilities, and the poem draws on these associations to express its themes through the particular qualities the bird represents.

The selected poem deals with culture as its central concern. The poem explores the cultural traditions, practices, and values of a particular community, examining how culture shapes identity and behavior. Whether celebrating, critiquing, or mourning cultural forms, the poem's primary engagement is with the cultural inheritance that defines a people and gives their lives their distinctive character.

The dominant images in The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born are those of filth and decay. Armah deliberately saturates the novel with images of rot, excrement, corruption, and physical degradation as a metaphor for the moral putrefaction of post-independence Ghanaian society. The filth and decay pervading the physical world of the novel mirror the moral decay of a society consumed by corruption and self-interest.

The title The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born implies that there is a possibility of moral regeneration in society. The beautiful ones, representing the honest, incorruptible individuals needed to lead Ghana, do not yet exist in the present corrupt environment, but the word yet carries the suggestion that they will eventually be born. The title holds out hope for future moral renewal even while lamenting its current absence.

In Lord of the Flies, the pig's skull regarding Ralph like one who knows all the answers suggests that Ralph was the only person with intuition and common sense left on the island. The skull's expression of knowing everything is ironically attributed to Ralph, the one boy who maintains rational thinking and moral clarity. He alone understands the danger they face, making the skull's all-knowing gaze a reflection of his own isolated comprehension.

The destruction of the conch along with Piggy's death in Lord of the Flies signifies degeneration into chaos. The conch had represented order, democracy, and civilized behavior throughout the novel, and its destruction marks the final collapse of the boys' attempt to maintain a civil society. With the conch gone and Piggy dead, all constraint and reason are eliminated, leaving only chaos.

In The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, the old man's faith referred to is Socialism. The novel engages critically with the ideology of Nkrumah's Ghana, which was built on socialist principles. The passage suggests that even the old man himself has doubts about the socialist doctrine he professes, reflecting the disillusionment with socialist ideology that pervades the novel's critique of post-independence politics.

The conversation in Lord of the Flies beginning I could swim when I was five, Daddy taught me occurs between Piggy and Ralph. This early exchange establishes the friendship and social dynamic between the two boys, with Piggy sharing personal information as he attempts to connect with Ralph. The question what's your father? reveals their contrasting backgrounds and sets up their relationship.

The image of Beelzebub in Lord of the Flies effectively captures the character of Jack. Beelzebub, the lord of the flies, is a name for the devil, and the pig's skull to which this name refers becomes associated with Jack's savage impulses and the evil that his descent into violence represents. Jack embodies the demonic force that Beelzebub symbolizes within the novel's moral framework.

The main significance of the fire in Lord of the Flies is to provide a signal for potential rescuers. The fire on the mountain is the boys' primary means of attracting passing ships and planes, and maintaining it represents their hold on civilization and their desire to be rescued. The fire's signal function makes it the most important practical and symbolic element in their survival strategy.

The poem now I fear disturbance of the quiet season, winter shall come bringing death from the sea, ruinous spring shall beat at our doors uses foreshadowing. The speaker anticipates and predicts future disasters: death from the sea, ruinous spring, and the destructive consequences of winter. This prediction of what is to come creates a sense of impending doom that is characteristic of foreshadowing as a literary device.

A novel that depicts the adventures of a main character who is usually something of a rogue is a picaresque. The picaresque novel originates in sixteenth-century Spain and features a witty, morally flexible protagonist who survives by their wits, moving through different social levels and episodic adventures. Characters like Tom Jones and Huckleberry Finn belong to this tradition.

An insincere literary work is known as a parody. A parody imitates another work's style and form without the genuine creative commitment of the original, using imitation for comic or critical purposes. The insincerity of parody lies in its refusal to take either itself or its subject seriously, making mockery through imitation rather than creating something authentically felt.

The technique used in bringing the plot of a play to an abrupt end is called deus ex machina. This device resolves an otherwise impossible dramatic situation by introducing an unexpected external force or agent that cuts through the complications of the plot. Its abruptness reflects its origins in classical theatre where a god was literally lowered by machine to resolve the play's conflicts.

In literature, a round character is associated with change and growth. Round characters are complex, fully realized individuals who develop over the course of a narrative, responding to events in ways that reveal psychological depth and the capacity for change. Unlike flat characters who remain static, round characters grow, learn, or are transformed by their experiences.

A play that tells a single story, has one setting, and takes place within a specified period is said to possess the unities. The classical unities of action, place, and time require dramatic works to be concentrated and unified in these three dimensions. A play that conforms to all three classical unities maintains a single plotline, a single location, and a timeframe typically no longer than a single day.

When words or phrases in either poetry or prose rise and fall measuredly, it is said that they have a regular rhythm. Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that creates a musical beat in language. When this pattern is regular and predictable, rising and falling in a measured way, it constitutes formal meter in poetry or rhythmic prose, creating a quality of ordered, musical movement.

The ode and the elegy are examples of lyrical poetry. Both forms are characterized by the expression of personal emotion and subjective experience that defines lyric poetry. The ode celebrates or meditates on a subject with heightened emotional intensity, while the elegy mourns loss. Both are lyrical because they prioritize the expression of the poet's feeling over narrative or dramatic elements.

In the passage, Joseph on the lower deck forgetting himself and living in his mind the sea life of light literature beforehand is day-dreaming. Joseph is mentally escaping his present circumstances by imaginatively projecting himself into the adventurous life he has read about in his books. This mental immersion in an imagined future or fictional world while physically doing nothing is characteristic of day-dreaming.

The passage about a man watching a faulty fan, turning to watch it rather than cutting off the sound in anger, each feeble movement increasing tension, creates a mood of suspense. The man's reluctance to act and his watchful waiting, combined with the fan's unpredictable movements, generate a tense, expectant atmosphere. The suspended action and the focus on the frustrating object create sustained suspense.

In the passage about the manager who was commonplace in complexion, feature, manners, and voice, the impression he creates in the narrator is of a hostile person. Despite his ordinary, unremarkable surface, something in his manner communicates an underlying hostility that is described as curious. This hidden antagonism beneath an unremarkable exterior defines his character as the narrator initially perceives it.

Ferdinand Oyono's description of the house dog that sprawled between the narrator's legs and followed each piece of fish with full envy indicates that the dog watched as his master ate the fish. The dog's envious gaze tracks every piece of food going into the host's mouth, and the dog is described as watching rather than acting on its desire, making watching its primary activity in the passage.

The passage reveals that Otto's wife was a potter in addition to being a wife and mother. Unlike the other women who defined themselves entirely through domestic roles, Otto's wife maintained a professional identity as a potter alongside her family roles. This combination, rather than substitution of one identity for another, is what distinguishes her from the other women described.

The passage about families who kept their feet from touching bottom during the great depression describes people who remained buoyant economically. The metaphor of keeping feet from touching bottom refers to staying financially afloat, not sinking into poverty. To remain buoyant economically means to maintain enough financial stability to survive without hitting rock bottom despite the severe economic pressures of the Depression.

The description of a man who sprung about the room in thick socks from fridge to bread bin to table, buttering and chopping and slicing and sprinkling, deft and efficient, conveys haste. The rapid movement from place to place, the list of simultaneous activities, and the word sprung all suggest rushed, energetic movement. The efficiency is the result of speed, and the overall impression is of someone moving with hasty purposefulness.

In Macbeth's soliloquy this supernatural soliciting cannot be ill, cannot be good, the supernatural fact that came true and is troubling Macbeth is his becoming Thane of Cawdor. The witches' prophecy that he would be Thane of Cawdor has just been fulfilled, and this event prompts Macbeth's troubled meditation: if the prediction was evil, why did it come true; if good, why does it disturb him?

The tone of the passage about virtue in Russia seeming to arise from men like a comforting body odour rather than coming from above is scathing. The comparison of virtue to body odour is deliberately degrading and mocking, reducing moral virtue to a physical, natural, and somewhat unpleasant emanation. This comparison expresses contempt for the kind of uncritical, instinctive morality being described.

Wole Soyinka's Post Mortem passage about the cold hands of death, the cotton-filled mouth, the brain on scales, and the question of whether it was a trick to prove foreknowledge after death depicts the ugliness of death. The physical details of the dead body, the cotton stuffing, the weighing of the brain, create a clinical, repellent image that foregrounds death's physical reality as ugly and undignified.

In The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, the discussion about the chichidodo bird that hates excrement but eats maggots that breed in it refers to The man. This ironic fable captures the man's contradictory position: he is disgusted by the corruption around him but benefits from the same system he despises, just as the chichidodo cannot avoid participating in what it claims to reject.

In The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, the use of the word salt is suggestive of an instrument of decay and of cleansing. Salt has dual properties: it preserves and cleanses, but it also erodes and destroys. In the novel's context, this ambivalence captures the moral complexity of life in a corrupt society where the same elements can simultaneously corrupt and cleanse, destroying what they preserve.

In Macbeth, the lines I think our country sinks beneath the yoke; it weeps, it bleeds, and each new day a gash is added to her wounds are spoken by Malcolm to Macduff. Malcolm is lamenting the state of Scotland under Macbeth's tyrannical rule, describing the country's suffering to Macduff in England. The extended metaphor of a wounded, weeping country expresses the depth of Scotland's oppression.

The selected poem portrays its subject as blood-thirsty. The character or force described in the poem is characterized by an excessive desire for violence, killing, and the shedding of blood. This blood-thirsty quality defines the subject's nature and actions, giving the poem a fierce, violent atmosphere and positioning the blood-thirsty force as dangerous and predatory.

In the selected poem, the imagery of the pauper reflects poverty and dirt. The physical description of the impoverished person combines the visual and sensory details of destitution with the physical dirtiness that accompanies severe poverty. Together these qualities, poverty and dirt, define the pauper's condition and create the poem's powerful image of material and physical degradation.

The dominant emotion expressed in the selected poem is grief. The poem dwells in the experience of profound loss and mourning, with imagery and language that convey deep sorrow. Whether mourning a person, a place, or a way of life, the pervasive grief shapes the poem's tone and makes it an expression of the emotional weight of irreversible loss.

The selected poem deals with the suffering of soldiers and civilians during a war. The poem addresses both those who fight and those who simply endure the consequences of conflict, recognizing that war's devastation extends beyond the battlefield to all who live within its reach. This inclusive perspective on wartime suffering gives the poem broad human relevance.

The selected poem expresses defiance and protest. The speaker's attitude toward the injustice or oppression being described is characterized by resistance and refusal to submit. Rather than accepting the situation or lamenting it passively, the poem strikes a tone of active defiance, asserting the right to resist and making a public protest against the conditions being challenged.

The dominant mood of the selected poem is melancholy. The poem is pervaded by a deep, sustained sadness that is not the acute grief of loss but the settled, quiet sorrow of someone who has come to terms with disappointment or the passage of time. This melancholic quality gives the poem a contemplative, autumnal atmosphere.

The dominant quality conveyed in the selected poem is coldness. Whether literally describing physical cold or using coldness as a metaphor for emotional distance, indifference, or inhospitality, the poem creates an atmosphere of chilly absence of warmth. This coldness permeates the poem's imagery and tone, creating an experience of chill and emotional frigidity.

The selected poem expresses a combination of fascination and fear. The subject of the poem inspires both attraction and terror in the speaker, creating a complex emotional response in which the desire to know or engage is inseparable from an instinctive apprehension. This ambivalent mixture of fascination and fear captures the experience of encountering something powerful and dangerous.

In The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, Kofi Billy's right leg was cut off by a machine because the young Englishman loaded too much tension into the steel ropes. This industrial accident, caused by the negligence or incompetence of the European overseer, is a specific instance of the exploitation and careless treatment of African workers that the novel critiques. The employer's recklessness causes permanent injury to the worker.

By the coup that takes place near the end of The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, Armah suggests that there is very little hope for genuine change. The overthrow of Nkrumah's corrupt government does not result in moral renewal but merely replaces one set of rulers with another. The military coup represents a change of faces rather than a change of values, confirming the novel's pessimistic vision of political life.

In The Beautiful Ones Are Not Yet Born, the remark that there is no difference between the whitemen and their apes reflects a reaction to the politics of betrayal. The African leaders who have replaced the colonizers behave just as exploitatively, leading the comparison of whitemen and their successors to be made in disgust. The politics of betrayal, in which independence leaders betray the promise of liberation, provokes this bitter observation.

In Lord of the Flies, the fact that the rescue ship was attracted not by a signal fire made for that purpose but by a fire set by Jack to hunt Ralph out is an oxymoron. The fire intended to kill Ralph paradoxically becomes the instrument of his rescue, combining two contradictory purposes in a single event. This contradiction is the defining quality of the oxymoron: two opposite effects arising from one act.

In Lord of the Flies, the island is a symbol of innocence. At the beginning, the island represents an untouched, pristine natural environment that seems to offer the boys an opportunity to create a better society than the adult world at war they have left behind. The island's initial beauty and abundance evoke the innocent state of humanity before the destructive impulses symbolized by Golding's boys take over.

In Lord of the Flies, Jack's act of painting his face can be interpreted to mean regression into savagery. The face paint acts as a mask that severs Jack from his civilized identity and allows the savage impulses within to emerge without inhibition. The paint transforms him from a schoolboy into a predatory hunter, symbolizing the abandonment of civilized restraint and the embrace of primitive, violent instincts.

The purgation of the emotions of pity and fear in tragedy is called catharsis. Aristotle introduced this concept in his Poetics to explain the psychological and moral effect of watching tragedy: the audience is moved to feel intense pity and fear by the protagonist's suffering, and through this emotional engagement, these emotions are purged or purified, leaving the audience in a state of emotional equilibrium.

The character in Lord of the Flies who best symbolizes man's pride in his ability to reason is Piggy. Piggy is the intellectual of the group, the boy who understands cause and effect, who insists on rational procedure, and who values the life of the mind. His glasses, which are used to start the fire, represent rational, scientific thinking, and his consistent appeal to reason makes him the novel's symbol of human intellectual capacity.

An exaggeration or overstatement in literature is a hyperbole. Hyperbole is a rhetorical and literary device that uses deliberate, extreme exaggeration to create emphasis or comic effect. Examples include I have told you a million times and she was the most beautiful woman in the world. Hyperbole intensifies meaning by exceeding what could literally be true, using extravagance to capture emotional reality.

A quatrain is a stanza consisting of four lines. The quatrain is one of the most common stanza forms in English poetry, used in sonnets (which consist of three quatrains and a couplet), ballads, and many other verse forms. Its four-line structure can accommodate various rhyme schemes, including alternating rhyme (abab), enclosed rhyme (abba), and simple paired rhyme (aabb).

The stylistic device that uses the name of one thing to describe another is called a metonym. Metonymy is a figure of speech in which a word or phrase associated with something is used to represent the thing itself. For example, the crown stands for monarchy, the pen for writing, and Washington for the US government. The name of one associated thing substitutes for the thing it represents.

A form of symbolism in which ideas or abstract qualities are represented in a poem is an allegory. Allegory extends symbolic representation throughout an entire narrative or poem, with each element systematically representing abstract ideas, moral qualities, or real-world situations. Unlike simple symbol, allegory involves a sustained, coherent system of parallels between the literal surface and the abstract meaning it represents.

The word image in literary criticism is associated with abstraction. An image in literature is a concrete representation, a picture created in words, but its function is to make abstract ideas tangible and accessible through concrete sensory detail. The image bridges abstraction and physical reality, giving abstract thoughts, emotions, or concepts a concrete form that readers can apprehend through their senses.

The poem let the greying day grow, let the evening horns blow, let the melting mountains go, let the sundown sow uses alliteration as its dominant device. The repeated g sound in greying, grow, and go, and the b and l sounds in blow and let, create patterns of consonantal repetition throughout the lines. This alliterative quality gives the poem its musical, incantatory rhythm.

In Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock, the lines whether the nymph shall break Diana's law, or some frail China jar receive a flaw, or stain her honour, or her new brocade use zeugma. The verb stain governs both honour and new brocade in different senses: staining honor is metaphorical while staining a brocade is literal. This yoking of disparate objects under a single verb in different meanings is characteristic of zeugma.

In James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, the word artificer refers to a craftsman. The phrase old father, old artificer alludes to Daedalus, the mythological craftsman who created wings. Stephen Dedalus uses this invocation to align himself with the creative craftsman of myth, asking for the skill of the maker rather than divine inspiration, emphasizing artistic creation as a form of skilled craft.

Faku's excitement about Garba's intention to marry her and settle in the city is optimistic. Her announcement is made with enthusiasm and hope, viewing the prospect of city life and marriage as positive developments that will improve her situation. This forward-looking, hopeful attitude toward what the future will bring defines her mood in this passage as optimistic.

Oswald Mtshali's description of the morning mist and chimney smoke of White City Jabavu flowing thick yellow as pus oozing from a gigantic sore is a graphic description. The detailed, visceral imagery of yellowish mist compared to pus from a wound creates a vivid, physically immediate picture of urban poverty and pollution. The graphic nature of the comparison does not spare the reader from the harsh reality being depicted.

In Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, going up the river was like traveling back to the earliest beginnings of the world, when vegetation rioted on the earth and the big trees were kings suggests that the environment is formidable. The ancient, primordial quality of the landscape, the rioting vegetation, and the dominance of enormous trees all create a sense of overwhelming, intimidating natural power that makes the environment formidable.

In Lord of the Flies, the slow deepening of silence until the click of the fire and the soft hiss of roasting meat could be heard clearly refers to the dropping of the fat of the meat in the fire. The specific sounds described, the clicking and hissing associated with cooking, are caused by the fat dripping from the roasting meat and hitting the hot fire below, producing the characteristic sounds of meat being cooked.

The passage about a road that was endless, where one road led to a thousand others, which fed into paths, tracks, and streets, describes urban disorder. The chaotic, labyrinthine quality of the road network, constantly branching and subdividing without clear direction or endpoint, represents the disorganized, overwhelming complexity of urban space. This description evokes the confusion and disorder characteristic of a city without clear planning.

The poem about a poor bastard dumped on the ground to make room for nocturnal fathers, spending horrid nights among steaming pots of food, describes squalor. The conditions of the child's existence, the discomfort, the degrading treatment, the physical wretchedness of sleeping among cooking pots, create a vivid image of extreme poverty, disorder, and deprivation that constitutes squalor.

In Soyinka's The Lion and the Jewel, the lines this is the words of women, at this moment our star sits in the center of the sky are spoken by Sadiku. Sadiku is Baroka's senior wife, and these words reflect her role as a spokesperson for the women of Baroka's household. Her invocation of the auspicious position of the star reveals a ceremonial or ritual moment in the play.

In Arms and the Man, Bluntschli's description of himself as a practical, matter-of-fact soldier reveals simplicity and naturalness. Unlike the romantic hero Sergius, Bluntschli has no illusions about war or himself. His frank, unpretentious self-presentation, free from military posturing or romantic idealism, reveals a character of straightforward honesty and natural, uncomplicated personality.

The main themes of Arms and the Man are best summed up by the phrase military glory and romantic love. The play satirizes both the glorification of war and the romantic idealization of love, exposing them as equally deluded fantasies. Shaw sets realistic common sense against both romantic heroism in battle and idealized courtly love, showing how illusion distorts both war and relationships.

In Soyinka's The Lion and the Jewel, the division used as a technical device to denote the symbolic significance of events is morning, noon and night. These three temporal divisions structure the play and carry symbolic weight: morning represents the beginning or youth, noon represents the fullness of day or maturity, and night represents conclusion or consummation. This temporal structure organizes the play's dramatic and symbolic progression.

In J.P. Clark's Streamside Exchange, the stream's movement is associated with the uncertainty of the future. The water's constant change, never the same from moment to moment, and its unknown destination make it a symbol for the unpredictable, unknowable quality of time ahead. The stream's uncertainty mirrors the speaker's apprehension about what lies ahead.

In Arms and the Man, Catherine's natural looks portray her as a sophisticated lady. Despite living in Bulgaria, Catherine aspires to and achieves the appearance of the fashionable, cultivated Western woman. Her natural appearance projects the image of a sophisticated lady, distinguishing her from the provincial mountain background of her actual life and reflecting her social aspirations.

In Arms and the Man, the line you know how to hurt with your tongue and with your hands refers to eavesdropping in the scene's context. The character is responding to having been overheard and confronted with something discovered through listening in on private conversations. Eavesdropping is the transgression that has brought this painful confrontation about, making it the relevant action being referenced.

The atmosphere of the poem Birdsong is one of sadness. Despite the typically joyful associations of birds and their song, the poem uses its imagery and tone to create a pervading sense of melancholy and grief. The birdsong in this poem becomes an expression of sorrow rather than joy, giving the poem a bittersweet or purely mournful atmosphere.

The poet's mood in the poem Garba is one of contentment. The speaker expresses a settled, peaceful satisfaction with their situation, free from desire for change or improvement. This contentment gives the poem a quiet, accepting quality, suggesting that the poet has found a state of sufficiency and does not yearn for more than the present provides.

In Arms and the Man, Raina's view is that if one is incapable of gratitude, he is incapable of any noble sentiment. Sentiment refers to feeling, particularly refined, elevated feeling that distinguishes cultured from base people. Raina links gratitude to the capacity for all noble feeling, suggesting that the inability to feel and express gratitude indicates a deficiency in the entire range of elevated human emotions.

The lines you just wait, I'll tell you more but let me first sell my tomatoes reflect reality. The speaker's practical interruption of their storytelling to attend to the actual business of selling vegetables grounds the exchange in ordinary, everyday life. The intrusion of commercial necessity into the narrative moment captures the reality of daily life, where practical needs interrupt and shape human communication.

In the poem Night, the people described are determined to give meaning to their life. Despite the darkness and difficulty of their situation, the poem shows individuals who refuse passive acceptance and instead choose active engagement with their existence. This determination to find or create meaning, even in adverse conditions, is the dominant quality that characterizes the people in the poem.

In Christopher Okigbo's Idoto, the word Idoto refers to a village stream. Idoto is the actual stream in Okigbo's home village of Ojoto in Anambra, Nigeria, associated with a water goddess of the same name. Okigbo returns imaginatively to this stream as a place of spiritual origin and renewal, and the poem's central act is the poet's return to worship before this sacred village waterway.

The technique Kwesi Brew uses in his poem involves gory details. The poem does not shy away from the explicit, bloody, or disturbing details of its subject matter, using graphic imagery of violence or suffering to make its impact. This unflinching use of gory detail gives the poem its visceral power and ensures that readers cannot distance themselves from the reality being described.

In the poem The Prodigals, the subjects are described as haughty. The characters depicted carry themselves with an air of superiority and disdain, looking down on others and refusing to lower themselves to ordinary standards of behavior or humility. This haughtiness is a defining characteristic that shapes both their behavior and the way others respond to them.

The poem Withering, burn, gho... deals with desolation. The imagery of withering, burning, and destruction creates an atmosphere of total abandonment and emptiness. Desolation, the state of being utterly abandoned and stripped of life or comfort, is the dominant experience the poem conveys through its imagery of destruction and waste.

In Arrow of God, the saying it is not bravery for a man to beat his wife and the subsequent comment about men and their wives quarreling refers to Akueke and her husband. This conversation relates to the domestic situation of Ezeulu's daughter Akueke and her troubled marriage, addressing the issue of domestic violence in the context of traditional Igbo values about proper and improper behavior between spouses.

In Arrow of God, the statement the new religion was like a leper means that if welcomed, the new religion will overshadow the traditional religions. Just as a leper, once given hospitality, tends to stay and cannot easily be removed, Christianity, once allowed to establish itself in the community, will grow and displace indigenous spiritual practices. The comparison warns against the long-term consequences of accommodation.

In Arrow of God, the statement that any yam harvest in the fields was harvested in the name of the son, following a conversion, refers to Jesus Christ. The son in this context is the Christian figure of the Son of God. After Christian conversion changes the ritual context of farming, the harvest is dedicated to Jesus Christ rather than to Ulu, the traditional deity, marking the displacement of indigenous religious practice by Christianity.

In Mariama Ba's So Long a Letter, the lines one is a mother to shield when lightning streaks the night and thunder shakes the earth occur after the confession of Ramatoulaye's daughter that she was pregnant. When her daughter reveals her pregnancy, Ramatoulaye responds with maternal protectiveness rather than condemnation, embodying the image of a mother as shield against life's storms for her child.

In Arrow of God, the saying that no man however great was greater than his people, and that no one ever won judgment against the clan, means that the individual should submit his will to that of the clan. This statement expresses the communal philosophy of Igbo society in which collective judgment and social harmony take precedence over individual pride or private ambition, no matter how powerful the individual.

In Arrow of God, the crisis over the New Yam Feast arose because Ezeulu's absence from Umuaro had prevented him from eating the sacred yams at the right time. As chief priest of Ulu, Ezeulu must eat one sacred yam each month to count the months. His detention in Okperi by the colonial administrator meant he could not perform this ritual on schedule, causing a delay that created a crisis for the entire community's harvest calendar.

In So Long a Letter, the statement a wife must understand once and for all and must forgive is attributed to Mawdo Ba, who uses it to justify his marrying young Nabou out of a sense of duty to his mother. Mawdo invokes this traditional expectation of wifely submission and forgiveness to rationalize his betrayal of Aissatou, framing his second marriage as something she is obligated to accept and excuse.

In So Long a Letter, the line if you can procreate without loving, merely to satisfy the pride of your declining mother is addressed to or about Aissatou. The statement is a response to Mawdo's marriage to young Nabou at his mother's insistence, and it represents Aissatou's standpoint: that procreation motivated by pride rather than love is unacceptable. Aissatou refuses to accept her husband's betrayal on these terms.

In So Long a Letter, the statement you forget that I have a heart, a mind, that I am not an object to be passed from hand to hand is addressed to Tamsir. This protest against being treated as a commodity to be disposed of without regard to her feelings is directed at Tamsir, who comes to propose marriage to Ramatoulaye after Modou's death, treating her as simply available rather than as a person with her own will and feelings.

Soliloquy is a term generally used in drama. A soliloquy is a dramatic device in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud on stage, alone or believing themselves to be alone, revealing their inner mental or emotional state directly to the audience. While poetry has monologue, the formal term soliloquy is specifically associated with theatrical performance.

In So Long a Letter, the line the sugar-daddy of the boutique dresses wants to marry Binetou reveals that the sugar-daddy is the speaker's father. The passage describes the announcement that a wealthy older man who buys boutique dresses wants to marry the young Binetou, and in the context of the story, this reveals a personal connection between the speaker and the man described, making the sugar-daddy a familial figure.

Blank verse consists of unrhymed five-stress lines. It is written in iambic pentameter, with each line containing five iambic feet (ten syllables in the pattern unstressed-stressed), but without end rhyme. Shakespeare used blank verse extensively for the speech of noble characters, and Milton wrote Paradise Lost in blank verse, making it the dominant form of serious English poetry from the Renaissance onward.

A burlesque is an exaggerated mockery of a literary work, style, or genre. Burlesque uses grotesque exaggeration, comic distortion, and satirical imitation to ridicule serious works or conventions by treating serious subjects trivially or trivial subjects with absurd dignity. Unlike subtle parody, burlesque is broad, physical, and often ribald in its comic approach.

One major narrative technique that a novel shares with drama is dialogue. Both novels and plays use dialogue as a primary means of revealing character, advancing plot, conveying information, and dramatizing conflict. While drama relies almost exclusively on dialogue and action, the novel incorporates dialogue as one of its key narrative tools alongside narration, description, and interior monologue.

The dum, dum of the drum is a good example of onomatopoeia. Onomatopoeia uses words whose sounds imitate the sounds they describe. The words dum dum reproduce the actual percussive sound of a drum being struck, creating an immediate auditory impression. The sound of the word and the sound being described are identical, which is the defining characteristic of onomatopoeia.

A stanza of three lines linked by rhyme is generally called a tercet. The tercet is a three-line stanza that can use various rhyme schemes, including the tripling scheme (aaa) or the interlocking rhyme scheme of terza rima (aba bcb cdc) used by Dante in the Divine Comedy. The tercet's compactness and triple rhythm give it a distinctive musical quality.

A speech made at the end of a dramatic performance is generally called an epilogue. The epilogue follows the main action of a play and serves to wrap up the story, reflect on its themes, address the audience directly, or request their approval. It contrasts with the prologue which opens the play. Some epilogues are spoken by a character; others by an actor stepping out of their role.

Assonance occurs when similar vowel sounds are repeated in a sentence or line of poetry. Unlike rhyme, which requires matching sounds at word endings, assonance creates internal vowel harmony throughout a line, as in fleet feet sweep and deep purple. This repetition of vowel sounds creates a musical quality that gives poetry its sonic richness without requiring full end rhyme.

The description of round cheeks, a round nose, and a round chin that were a cool, healthy red, all perfectly circular, is an example of photographic clarity. The precise, detailed description of the face captures its features with the exact, objective specificity of a photograph, rendering every dimension with meticulous accuracy. This photographic clarity gives the passage its vivid, lifelike quality.

The lines from the island of Fogo, the palm trees are slow singers of farewell, and the sail on the sea writes use personification. The palm trees are given the human ability to sing, and the sail on the sea is given the ability to write. These human activities attributed to natural phenomena are characteristic of personification, which animates the natural world with human capacities.

The verse here lies a great and mighty king, whose promise none relies on, he never said a foolish thing, nor ever did a wise one is an epitaph. An epitaph is an inscription written for a tombstone or in memory of someone deceased. This verse is a satirical epitaph, praising and damning the king in the same breath, creating a memorable critical summary of a ruler's life and legacy.

The lines see how she leans her cheek upon her hand, O that I were a glove upon that hand from Romeo and Juliet use apostrophe. Romeo addresses Juliet as if directly speaking to her from his hiding place below, though she cannot hear him. He speaks to her presence from a distance, addressing her as if she were aware of him, which is the defining gesture of apostrophe.

The poem about Akosua Nowa and the red ant on the tree is memorable for its extended images of treasure and gun. The poem develops metaphors and images of wealth and weaponry that run through its lines, creating an extended figurative pattern. The sustained development of these images through the poem gives it its distinctive quality of extended, elaborated imagery.

The passage about Trinidad being too unimportant suggests that the island was so small that its people did not value its history. The inhabitants' sense of their island's insignificance in the larger world meant that they did not regard their own history as worth preserving or celebrating. This self-perceived smallness translated into a lack of historical consciousness and self-worth.

The passage a great city is a battlefield, you need to be a fighter to live in it, not merely exist but live, uses symbolism. The city is symbolically represented as a battlefield, with the metaphor extending into the comparison between merely existing and truly living as analogous to surviving versus thriving in combat. This sustained symbolic equation of urban life with warfare carries meanings beyond the literal comparison.

In Soyinka's The Lion and the Jewel, Lakunle is presented as a caricature of a modern educated man. His adoption of Western ideas is superficial and ridiculous, combining genuine educational aspiration with comic ignorance of how to apply it. Soyinka uses him to satirize the type of educated African who has absorbed the surface manners of Western civilization without its substance or wisdom.

In The Lion and the Jewel, the lines I am the twinkle of a Jewel but he is the hind-quarters of a lion suggest that Sidi is superior to the Bale. Sidi compares herself, with irony, to the bright jewel while dismissively comparing Baroka to the undignified rear end of a lion. Despite the apparent self-deprecation in calling herself only a twinkle, her description of Baroka as the hind-quarters actually reveals her sense of her own greater worth.

In The Lion and the Jewel, the lines but there have been no new reeds cut by his servants, no new cots woven means that no children have been born recently. New cots are needed for babies, and the absence of new cots being woven indicates that no births have occurred in the Bale's household. This is evidence supporting the rumor of the Bale's impotence, as the absence of baby preparations suggests no new children are expected.

The central theme of The Lion and the Jewel is the clash between tradition and modernity. The play dramatizes the conflict between traditional African values, represented by the Bale Baroka, and Western-influenced modernization, represented by the schoolteacher Lakunle. Sidi's choice between these two worlds, and the ultimate triumph of traditional values, make this conflict the play's central concern.

In Arms and the Man, Petkoff asking Sergius to tell Catherine about the queer story his friend told them creates irony. The story concerns a soldier who hid in Raina's room, a detail that Petkoff and Sergius do not connect to their own household. The irony arises because the audience and the women present know the full truth while the men remain oblivious, making their casual storytelling ironically fraught.

In Arms and the Man, Raina demonstrated her love for Captain Bluntschli by giving him her portrait with an inscription. This romantic gesture, inscribing a portrait to the man who had sheltered in her room, is Raina's most explicit declaration of feeling for Bluntschli. When Bluntschli reveals he still has the portrait at the end of the play, it confirms the reality and depth of her attachment.

In The Lion and the Jewel, the lines he risked his life that you may boast a warrior-hunter for your lord are addressed to the mummers who dance in mockery of the Bale's rumoured impotence. The mummers are the performers who enact the satirical mime commenting on Baroka's perceived weakness. The irony is that they mock the Bale's virility while he will ultimately prove them wrong.

In Arms and the Man, the way Louka carries out her duties as a maid can be characterized as bold and self-assured. Unlike a deferential servant, Louka carries herself with confidence and a sense of her own worth. She is not cowed by her position, and her boldness in her interactions with both the family and Sergius reflects her sense of personal dignity and her ambitions beyond the servant class.

The poem about tide and market suggests the constancy of nature. Just as tides follow predictable patterns regardless of human activity, and market days occur in regular cycles, the poem uses these natural and social rhythms to express the reliable, unchanging quality of the natural world. This constancy contrasts with the impermanence of human affairs, providing a stable backdrop to human experience.

In Arms and the Man, when Raina describes a soldier as a regular handsome fellow with flashing eyes, the tone is one of mockery. She is reporting or remembering the description of Sergius in battle as a romantic hero, but the stylized, operatic quality of the description, describing him like an operatic tenor, reveals that she is ironically or sarcastically rendering the theatrical heroism she has been taught to admire.

The word naked in the selected poem conveys reverence. In spiritual and ritual contexts, nakedness can represent vulnerability before the divine, a stripping away of all pretension to stand honestly before sacred power. The nakedness described in the poem carries a quality of humble, open devotion rather than shame or sensuality, giving the word a sacred, reverential significance.

The selected poem about when the dead come reveals our inability to understand our ancestors. The poem explores the difficulty of communicating across the divide between the living and the dead, suggesting that despite the dead's attempts to reach us, we lack the capacity or wisdom to receive what they try to convey. This failure of understanding reflects a broader cultural disconnection from ancestral wisdom.

Gabriel Okara's poem presents inspiration as its central concern. The poem explores the sources and nature of creative or spiritual inspiration, addressing what motivates and energizes the creative impulse. Okara's work often engages with the relationship between African tradition and modern experience, and this particular poem uses its imagery to express what inspires the artistic or spiritual life.

The selected poem about the African experience suggests the lack of a clear sense of direction coupled with years of oppression that weakened the will. The poem addresses the uncertainty and purposelessness resulting from colonialism's psychological damage, which left Africans without clear cultural bearings. Years of oppression undermined the confidence and direction needed to move forward with conviction.

Theo Luzuka's poem is classified as a gossip. The poem takes the form of casual, informal talk about other people's affairs, using the social form of gossip as its vehicle for commentary. This gossipy quality gives the poem its intimate, chatty tone and allows it to make observations about social behavior through the informal channels of community talk rather than formal poetic address.

The Fulani Creation Story teaches that death came into the world when man set himself up as God's rival. In the story, the sequence of creation culminates in man's prideful challenge to the divine, and it is this act of hubris, attempting to equal or surpass God, that introduces death into existence. The moral is that human pride and rivalry with the divine bring mortality as their consequence.

The selected poem about white flowers suggests that nature is indifferent to man's predicament. Despite human suffering, nature continues its cycles unmoved, neither sympathizing with nor acknowledging human pain. The white flowers blooming regardless of the human drama around them exemplify this indifference, suggesting that the natural world has no concern for the particular troubles of human beings.

In Arrow of God, the statement this madness which they say you have must now begin to know its bounds, addressing Ezeulu's behavior, is hyperbolic. The accusation of madness exaggerates Ezeulu's independent-mindedness and refusal to submit to communal pressure, using extreme language (madness) to describe what is actually strong-willed resistance. This exaggerated characterization of principled behavior as insanity is hyperbole.

In Arrow of God, the immediate cause of the war between Umuaro and Okperi was the land dispute. The two communities had a longstanding disagreement over a piece of land, and when Akukalia, Umuaro's envoy, desecrated Okperi's sacred objects during negotiations, it triggered the outbreak of actual war. The land dispute was the underlying and immediate cause of the conflict.

In Arrow of God, Ezeulu's mood when locked up in Okperi by the white colonial administrator is one of indifference. Despite being detained and effectively removed from his duties, Ezeulu maintains a philosophical detachment and refusal to be broken by his imprisonment. This indifference is part of his sense of his own dignity and his understanding that the gods will vindicate him regardless of what men do to him.

In Arrow of God, the saying it is good for a misfortune like this to happen once in a while, so that we can understand refers to the outrage which Oduche committed against the sacred python. The incident of Oduche trapping the sacred python in a box has caused a community crisis, and this philosophical response to the misfortune suggests that such shocks, though painful, serve a purpose in clarifying values and testing the community's commitment to its traditions.

In So Long a Letter, the source of Aissatou's success in life is her social connections. Rather than relying on masculine support or favorable circumstances, Aissatou builds her life through the relationships and connections she establishes within the wider society. Her ability to cultivate meaningful social networks, combined with her personal strength, enables her to achieve independence and success after leaving Mawdo.

In So Long a Letter, Aunty Nabou's subtle influence over young Nabou was developed through family ties. Aunty Nabou shapes her niece by invoking the bonds of family obligation and traditional values about a woman's duty to her clan.
